source_text: Porro utatur indicio epistolae, qua aut accepit, aut finxit me responsionem contra novos Manichaeos (quia vetus dedignatur videri) quattuor voluminibus explicasse; cur non curavit ea quae obiecissemus addiscere? Cur non studuit, qui cum esset congressurus, agnoscere; sed levitate turpissima concitatus in certamen maximum luminibus involutis, Andabatarum more, processit? Quod factum eiusmodi allegatione defendit, ut dicat se patroni sui festinationem, quam ille in transmittendis schedis habuit, imitari praecipiti responsione voluisse; quasi non honestissime potuerit intimare tempus sibi aliquod debere concedi, quo ad lectionem editi operis perveniret; flagitium esse inter eruditos in scribendi gravitate delinquere, et impatientia deliberandi impugnare, quod nescias. Huc accedit, quod nobis calliditatis moliturus invidiam, quae dictorum eius seriem curtaverit, his excerptis fidem accommodavit, quae verisimilius falsitate eius et malignitate, quam cuiusquam nostrum imperita simplicitate videntur esse composita. Verum id quovis animo, quovis auctore contigerit; nobis tamen duobus suffragatur modis; quia simul patuit et quanta sit levitas, et quanta imbecillitas in veritatis inimico, qui se approbavit, et cum loqui non debeat, tacere non posse, et paucis semiplenis discerptisque magis quam aggregatis sententiis, de primo tamen solum libro meo ita cessisse fractum, ut vulgi in nos femineis admodum vocibus pectora commoveret; quod disputationis nostrae processibus apparebit.
pass_a_gloss: Further, let him use the evidence of the letter by which he either received or invented that I had unfolded an answer against the new Manichaeans (because he disdains to seem an old one) in four volumes; why did he not take care to learn those things which we had objected? Why did he not study to know the one with whom he was going to clash; but, stirred by most base levity, went forward into a very great contest with eyes wrapped, after the manner of the Andabatae? Which deed he defends by an allegation of this kind, that he says he wanted to imitate by a headlong answer the haste of his patron, which that man had in sending across the sheets; as if he could not most honorably have intimated that some time ought to be granted him, by which he might come to the reading of the published work; that it is a disgrace among the learned to fail in the gravity of writing, and by impatience of deliberating to attack what you do not know. Add to this, that, about to work up ill-will against us for cunning which had shortened the series of his sayings, he lent faith to these excerpts which more probably seem composed by his falsehood and malice than by the unskilled simplicity of any of us. But however it happened, with whatever mind, with whatever author; it nevertheless supports us in two ways; because at once it lay open both how great is the levity and how great the weakness in the enemy of truth, who proved himself both unable to be silent even when he ought not to speak, and, by a few half-full sentences, torn apart rather than gathered, from my first book only, to have yielded so broken that he would move the breasts of the crowd against us with thoroughly womanish voices; which will appear by the processes of our disputation.

pass_b_english: Let him nevertheless use the evidence of the letter from which he learned, or invented, that I had set out a reply in four volumes against the new Manichaeans, since he disdains to be regarded as an old one. Why did he not take care to learn what objections we had made? Why did he not make an effort to know the person he was going to engage? Instead, driven by the most disgraceful frivolity, he entered a mighty contest with his eyes covered, like a blindfolded gladiator. He defends this behavior by saying that he wanted his hasty reply to imitate the haste with which his patron had sent the sheets. As though he could not most honorably have explained that he needed some time to obtain and read the published work! Among educated people it is disgraceful to fail in the seriousness writing demands and, through an unwillingness to deliberate, to attack something you do not know. Moreover, while planning to make us hated for the alleged cunning with which we had shortened the sequence of his words, he trusted excerpts that seem more likely to have been composed through his own falsehood and malice than through anyone on our side being innocently unskilled. Whatever the motive, and whoever the author, the occurrence supports us in two ways. It has revealed at once both the frivolity and the weakness of truth's enemy. He has shown that he cannot keep silent even when he ought not to speak, and that a few incomplete sentences, torn apart rather than assembled, drawn only from my first book, defeated and broke him so thoroughly that he tried to stir up the populace against us with thoroughly womanish cries. The course of our discussion will make this clear.

choices.why: Julian's standing charge: natural evil is Manichaean. Keep the sect-name, not 'dualists'.
Julian's name for the doctrine he attacks: evil as a nature rather than as will.
